If we use all the documents in the large corpus, even those that are not relevant, the results of the model may not be accurate.
But if we only use the documents that we know are relevant, we may be missing information that is useful.
To find the solution, we propose a method called 'Adaptive Ensembling' that can select which documents are most useful from a large corpus.
We tested it with some experiments that showed that it can work for political document analysis.
**Background:** In many cases of text classification in political science, the models of classification are trained with a lot of data and it is good data.
But when the model is used for a new text that it has not seen before, it may not work well because the data was not like the new text.
This is called a problem of 'domain adaptation'.
We need a new model that can work in a new place with a new text even if the new text is not like the old text.
We also need a model that can make the best use of the data, so that even the data that we are not sure if it is good or not can be used.
**Method:** We made a new method called 'Adaptive Ensembling'.
It is a type of 'unsupervised domain adaptation' that can select which documents are most useful from a large corpus.
It does this by finding the features of the documents that we know are most important, so that we can use all the other documents.
